title: Netflix's 'Best of the Best' Brings College Bollywood Dance to the World
excerpt: Six years after pitching a love letter to the college desi dance circuit, Hasan Minhaj's Bollywood-fusion comedy — starring Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia and directed by Lena Khan — arrives on Netflix on September 18.
body:
• Best of the Best, billed as America's first collegiate Bollywood dance musical competition film, starts streaming on Netflix on Friday, September 18, 2026.
  • Co-writers Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam built the film from their own college dance-circuit years; Minhaj calls the six-year project a "labor of love."
  • The title honors a real University of Michigan competition founded by Palak Sheth that ran until 2012.
  • Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia star as best friends Maya and Anjali; Lena Khan directs.

A six-year labor of love arrives on Netflix

Six years after Hasan Minhaj started pitching it — the same year his son was born — Best of the Best begins streaming on Netflix on Friday, September 18, 2026. The Bollywood-fusion dance comedy, directed by Lena Khan and co-written by Minhaj with longtime collaborator Prashanth Venkataramanujam, follows two childhood best friends who join a cutthroat college dance team and learn the road to nationals is far more ruthless than expected.

Ramakrishnan (Never Have I Ever) and Kedia play Maya and Anjali, whose disastrous high-school talent-show routine went viral in the worst way. At UCLA they join the university's nationally ranked Bollywood-fusion dance team, where rivalries and academic pressure strain their friendship — especially when Anjali is unexpectedly chosen as team lead instead of Maya — before the pair reconcile ahead of their final performance.

In press interviews ahead of the release, the cast has framed the film as a tribute to the real college dance world rather than a spoof of it. Minhaj also plays college professor Hamza Latif.

"I've watched my son grow up while making this. He was born when we first pitched this, and he's six years old now. So this was a labor of love."

— Hasan Minhaj, co-writer, co-star and producer

Context & Background

The idea grew from the writers' college years. Minhaj competed in Bollywood-inspired dance competitions at UC Davis, Venkataramanujam at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. After the emotionally exhausting run of Patriot Act, the pair wanted something joyful — a coming-of-age comedy that led them to the dance teams, per Netflix Junkie's account of Minhaj's comments to Netflix's Tudum, which he described as a love letter to the college years when South Asian students see their culture, and Bollywood dance, celebrated.

The title is a mark of honor. Best of the Best was a real competition created by Palak Sheth — now director of privacy and public policy at Meta — during her dancing years at the University of Michigan, built to bring dance styles from different Indian states onto one stage. It ended in 2012, but the film keeps both its name and its spirit of unity, according to Her Campus.

The project began at Amazon MGM under the working title For the Culture before Netflix picked it up; it is a Bollywood-fusion dance comedy, not a traditional Bollywood production. Production took place in New Jersey, though the story is set at UCLA. For Ramakrishnan — who had never danced competitively — the role meant months of intensive training, per Mogaz.

Impact & Analysis

"We were pushing this rock uphill, trying to get America's first collegiate Bollywood dance musical competition film made," Minhaj told PEOPLE. Early reviews suggest the effort reads on screen: Nerdtropolis called it "a wonderful celebration of Bollywood cinema through the Gen Z college experience," praising its dance sequences, while the New York Times headlined its review "They Think They Can Dance."

"We were pushing this rock uphill, trying to get America's first collegiate Bollywood dance musical competition film made. And that's all I was focused on."

— Hasan Minhaj, to PEOPLE

Per Netflix Junkie, the film's models range from To All the Boys I've Loved Before to Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, and its ensemble mixes established names — Lilly Singh, Janina Gavankar, Chaneil Kular, Nico Greetham — with professional dancers and newcomers.

Diaspora Angle

For many South Asian American students, the collegiate dance circuit was never a sideshow — it was the social and cultural center of campus life. By placing that world at the center of a mainstream Netflix comedy, the film treats a defining diaspora institution as heroic rather than exotic. As Minhaj told PEOPLE: "You're never going to get the specificity unless you take the responsibility yourself."

What's Next

The film streams today on Netflix, and its opening-weekend performance will be closely watched — a strong Top 10 showing would signal appetite for more South Asian-led ensemble stories beyond prestige drama. Either way, Minhaj's six-year bet has changed the template, proving a joyful, unapologetically desi campus story can get made. With a built-in audience of former collegiate dancers across the country, the film's loudest champions may be off-screen.
